utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. Please sit down. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. The Court Usher, I think, will assist you with the earphones. I hope you will not lose them. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I greet everyone. Let there be peace to this house and I hope that this day of trial as well as all of the proceedings may finish in accordance with God's will rather than as I wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, in e-court we had document number 5800; 65 ter 5800. Thank you. The Presiding Judge asked whether we would tender it or not. Before I tendered it, we will now look at the last page of this document so that you can see the signature. It was Manojlo Milovanovic, and we will also read the last sentence of this paragraph. I quote the last sentence: "You shall give permission to cross the front line only to those commissions for exchange of prisoners of war that announce their activity to the VRS Main Staff through the central commission of the exchange of prisoners of war with the consent and approval of the command of the chief of the VRS who are responsible for approving crossing the front line." Was everyone aware that the Main Staff commander was supposed to approve the crossing of the front lines at the request of the corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 21, line 25, Mr. Thayer asked you what was the role of the Main Staff in organising and carrying out the exchange. My question is this: If the Main Staff had to approve of any activity, did it have to receive a request for such activities from the corps and all other elements that had been agreed on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always did it that way on our side. We would send proposals and we would wait for approval. Without approval, we didn't go to carry out the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it safer for the commission when it had guarantees of both staffs to cross the front line rather than cross the front line when they didn't have such an approval?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never thought about that, whether it was safer or not, but we observed the orders. We were trying to have lull at the front lines so it was up to the corps. They were one across the other, and they had to agree among themselves and they had to create a lull on the front lines, so we did not have much illusions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. While reading a document, 03978, Mr. Thayer quoted the following to you; item 1 of this document on the exchange of prisoners says: "We agree that members of the commissions for the exchange of POWs from the Drina Corps and the Eastern Bosnia Corps should establish contact at the front line with representatives for the exchange of POWs from the 2nd Muslim Corps." Did I write here, because I signed this document, that I approved this or that we approved it? We agree? Does it mean that the Main Staff agreed or that an individual agreed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, in a place called Memici, we held two or three meetings with the commission of the Drina Corps, and from the other side was the commission from the Tuzla canton, that is to say, the 2nd Corps of the BH Army. But we didn't manage to achieve anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, the document 65 ter 3978 is now P2272. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would tender this document into evidence, and then I would call up another one in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Mitrovic: Did you see this document signed by General Milovanovic before today or before yesterday at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it was addressed to the Eastern Bosnia Corps, then it is probable that I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go back, please, to the document 65 ter 5800. My question I put to you, sir, was in relation to this document of the 29th of September, 1993, from the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska, to the Central Commission for Exchange of Prisoners of War and Civilians and to the command of the Drina Corps. Have you ever seen this before? Especially at the relevant time, when you were involved in these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember having seen it because it's a document from 1993, the 29th ... I would have to have a look at it to try and refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We dealt with this document already yesterday and we have seen it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I am familiar with it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Again, this document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5800 shall be assigned Exhibit P2272. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why a P document and not at D document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour, D278. Exhibit D278. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. At the moment, we are in cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we please show document Exhibit 7325 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, yesterday, on page 34, line 19 of the transcript, you said the following: "It was agreed in Geneva, between Alija Izetbegovic, Radovan Karadzic, and Tudjman, all for all, except those who had been criminally prosecuted. The Muslims and the Croats prosecuted everyone and the Serbs didn't," and so on. Do you remember that you said that yesterday during the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say so yesterday. I did not have this document in my hands, but as soon as I was appointed in mid-March 1993, I was informed about that, and certain measures were taken in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said yesterday when talking about this, that the Croats and the Muslims always said that those you requested from the list were being criminally prosecuted; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All our prisoners, unless an exchange was quickly carried out, were criminally prosecuted. It was a rare occasion that someone was not criminally prosecuted. Later on, this did not create any possible -- any great difficulties for exchange, if we had anyone to exchange, but early on, it was, because the rule was that those who were criminally prosecuted could not be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mitrovic, you can see here in front of you a document from the Main Staff, which is addressed to the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska, the Ministry of the Interior, and the security department of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the Drina Corps, and the Herzegovina Corps, as well as to the security department of the Eastern Bosnia Corps for information. In it, Colonel Beara also proposes to set up teams which would investigate criminal responsibility. We'll look at paragraph 4 now. And this is what he says. I quote: "Security" -- It's the second page in English; I apologise. "The security organs of the brigades should immediately send precise detainee lists to the security administration of the Main Staff of the VRS with general background information and a brief note on information relating to crimes against the Serbian people. We also ask the organs of the state security department of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska to do the same. Also, for every detainee, it should be mentioned if a criminal report has been filed against him and, if so, to which organ of justice; that is to say, to what extent have the crimes committed against the Serbian people have been documented, allowing for a criminal report to be submitted." This is my question: Were you also requested to provide such information from the centres where prisoners were being held; and did you know that information about those who had committed crimes against the Serbian people were collected on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we had but few prisoners, and that was in 1995, we had no instances of prisoners being interviewed and criminal reports filed. However, whoever happened to find themselves in Batkovici -- these were not war crimes. But we did the same as the other side did. We did file criminal reports. So formally, they were prosecuted, just so that it wouldn't happen that we cannot receive anyone and that we had to release everyone. It is it probable that units from other corps did this, because, before a person or, rather, a detainee, was sent to the Batkovici collection centre, if that happened, he was interviewed, statements were taken, and the measures that could be taken, in accordance with the law, were, indeed, taken so that there was no need to interview such persons in Batkovici again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The document says "for your information." I mean the Eastern Bosnia Corps. Tell me, did Milenko Todorovic or other security organs inform you that all those who had committed crimes against the Serbian people should be criminally prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did inform us. Only we did not have such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would tender this document into evidence so that we could move to the next one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could I please see the last page of it. It is signed by Colonel Beara. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, you indicated that this is 65 ter 7325. With this number, it is not included in the documents to be used during your cross-examination. Does this document have another number? I never know if this is the only number. If not, it will be received, but I would like to remind you to include all documents into your list so -- in order to enable the Prosecution to prepare the re-examination. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is our mistake. Initially, we intended to use this document with another witness but it turned out that this one was more favourable. It was a decision we made just prior, immediately prior to this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to receive the document number, the D number, by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 7325 shall be assigned Exhibit D279. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, on page 2, line 6, Mr. Thayer asked you to say something about the command structure of the Eastern Bosnia Corps and whether you dealt with exchanges of both prisoners and bodies.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look at video footage, which mentions both the corpses and those killed ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at 12 minutes, 9 seconds, and proceed to 12 minutes 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is this P991? You should please always indicate the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 1D801.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 1D801 is a surrogate sheet, but not a video, according to your list of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, you -- I was informed by the Registrar that the sheet doesn't indicate precisely which part of the video would -- would be part of this document. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will use only certain segments of the footage with this witness. It is our intention, though, that to have the entire video footage tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My problem was a different one. You just mentioned here a surrogate sheet with a specific number but without indication what it refers to. But go ahead and show us the video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, did you hear a moment ago what the person in uniform said when discussing things with those also present in the footage?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go back to 12 minutes, 9 seconds, to try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Try and listen carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, when you speak, you should switch on your microphone. But I would like to state that you stopped at 12 minutes, 37 seconds. The problem is, we don't -- and the Registry didn't receive a transcript of this footage, and there's no translation in English. And the Registry didn't receive a CD of this footage. I just noted that for the record. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could I read out what the people on the footage are saying? These are usually simple sentences and short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be more helpful if you asked the witness what he understood, because the witness is here to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I asked him what he was able to hear. And now he is about to tell us which will be interpreted in the absence of a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, can you tell us what the people in the footage were discussing? Could you hear some of the questions and some answers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question put was what their assessment was of how many of their people were killed from Srebrenica, when crossing over. I don't know whether this was already in free territory. In any case, the answer provided by another person, another fighter, was that he believed there were between 2- and 3.000 killed en route from Srebrenica. That's how I understood the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Your understanding is the same as mine. This is actually when they managed to reach Nezuk following their route through RS territory. My question is this: After the events in Srebrenica, did the Muslim Commission ask to receive the bodies of those who were killed during the break-through and in the area of the corridor?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us next look at 17 minutes to 17 minutes, 57 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We stopped at 17 minutes, 56 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, could you hear the conversation between the two people, given the fact that they were moving, walking all along?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe a question was put on how many of their people were killed, and the answer provided was between 2- and 3.000. I just wanted to ask you this: It is an area of Srebrenica and the area of the Drina Corps. Perhaps it would be better to put these questions to the witnesses who will testify about that area. You also asked me whether the other side asked to receive the bodies of their killed fighters. I would also say that someone from the Drina Corps would be better placed to answer that. They could have asked me to obtain those bodies, but ultimately it was only the Drina Corps who could provide the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. You are the only commission chairman brought here as a Prosecution witness. If it is difficult for you to answer these questions, I can only tell you that it is even more difficult for me to defend myself from these accusations. I am sorry to put you on the spot when I ask you about these people's conversation. But, yesterday during examination-in-chief, you said that there were killings amongst themselves. And when you were asked about it, you said that you only knew that there were such cases but that you had no detailed knowledge. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I don't know. It was in the media. They reported that there were mutual killings. As for any assessments I didn't pay attention to those. It was not in the area of responsibility of my corps, and I couldn't offer any contribution. That's why I only listened to it or read it very briefly. In any case, it was present in the RS media, as well as in the Federation. Articles were written about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic, for this answer. Let us move on with the footage to see what we can hear at 19 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we play that part, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, since we don't have a translation, can you tell us what you could make out of what the wounded person on the stretcher was saying?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood partially, and I don't even know who it refers to. He mentioned someone with four bullet belts across the chest and an M84 machine-gun, which is the latest model.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, I stopped you. You are overlapping again. Please wait until the translation has stopped. It is very difficult for the interpreters and the court recorder. You stopped at 19 minutes, 50 seconds, if I'm not mistaken. We're now back at the beginning of this part. I think at 18:59, that was the beginning of this footage, and it stopped at 19:50. You always should indicate where you stop, Mr. Tolimir. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stopped at 19 minutes, 47 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, can you recall what these people were discussing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a problem to recall what I could hear, but my hearing is not that well. And I can't understand them; that's the real problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only heard the latest part, and there seems to be a pass they crossed, but I couldn't make out the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the footage and the sound is not good enough, let us move to 33 minutes, 2 seconds. We won't replay this part because the witness cannot understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you also please turn the volume up to make it easier for the witness who can't hear that well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Usher just did it. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We stopped at 33 minutes, 49 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you make out any of what the collocutors were saying?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could. One would conclude that these are members of the Army of BiH. They were discussing what the situation was like in their ranks following the break-through, or during the break-through. They said that one of them activated a hand-grenade, killing himself, and wounding other ten people. Another person fired a burst of gun-fire; another one killed himself with a handgun. This is what I could understand from what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Does this confirm what you said, namely, that you heard that sometimes they killed one another or that there were suicides? What you heard in the media and in the public, is it confirmed by what is said here in this film?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could hear that in the media, but I would like to testify about what I personally experienced and saw, because that is the truth. And as for the media, sometimes they might show things differently, whatever it was. This is why I never liked to take representatives of the media to negotiations with me, because I was afraid that they might add something that was never said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't press you to say anything. I'm just asking you about what you said. My question is this: Considering that you have now seen sections from video footage, one part which you understood, the other which you didn't, did you understand that during the movements of these columns there were casualties on various locations about these persons speak [as interpreted]? Were you requested to retrieve bodies of those who had been killed from any location?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My commission never received such requests to collect bodies from any location, in this case from around the time of the fall of Srebrenica. We were never requested to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know whether the Joint Commission meetings which you attended, the Drina Corps or any other who was present during the exchanges with you, was ever requested to do that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time around Srebrenica, the meetings of the Drina Corps Commission and the Eastern Bosnia Corps Commission did not have any more meetings with the commission from the Tuzla canton or the 2nd Corps of the BH Army. We had separate meetings, and the 1st Krajina Corps also did. But we had no contacts with others, nor did anyone request any meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at D269. And then we won't look at any more documents dealing with Srebrenica. Thank you. So in e-court, we need to see D269. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see, and you are familiar with this, as you were an organ of the state security, it is a note from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior, State Security Service, the state security department and sector, Tuzla. It is it an Official Note on an interview about a person. I'm not going to read the person [as interpreted] because this is confidential information. The person told them how it was on the way through the corridor and where are the locations, where those who had lost their lives can be found. This is my question: There were similar notes. As a former organ of the State Security Service, can you tell us what is the credibility of such an Official Note, when a statement is taken from a person by an organ of the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important in the sense that, if there is anything incriminating or if there are any grounds to suspect that someone committed a crime, then it changes into a statement, and the person is criminally prosecuted. This is most often the initial document. The Official Notes are the first documents that are produced. And then the superior officer who is in charge decides what should be done; are any activities to be undertaken in connection with this Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Do state security organs have to write the truth about what such persons tell them; and is it equally credible as a statement given to public security; or does it have a greater degree of credibility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A document which is formed in the state security, until it becomes final and valid, has to be checked so that, always, whether a person was security checked or not, as a rule, around three sources were important and had to be interviewed so that something that is written would be considered correct, and that was this peacetime, when I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it then be logical that in wartime more than three sources were checked, or two, or that through another source what they say should be checked and only then would be considered credible, just as in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, a note as a note is just the initial document. It is taken as someone speaks. Checks are not waited for in order to draft it. And something may be done in connection with it. A superior officer signs it, and perhaps certain activities need to be carried out. It was like that at the time when I worked there. But in wartime, it's possible that things were organised differently, just like everything else was different than in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell us whether, when taking such notes, the state security organ who is making the note and taking the statement from a person is responsible for its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They are not to be held responsible. Their duty is to note what is being said. It is true that an interview is conducted before a note is made, and, of course, the operative, or the superior officer who is conducting the interview, has to estimate the person, the validity of the information, for his own sake and for possible criminal prosecution. And so that he wouldn't write all kinds of things that are of no use and cannot be used in the usual manner. So what is noted down is what the person who is interviewed says, and then later on it is checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see page 2 of this note.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As you said that at least three sources were necessary to confirm what is said, we'll now look at what this notes contains. Line 13 from above, where there's the number of 10.000 and underlined in black. And then around the middle it begins in line 13, I quote: "The source emphasises that on that occasion about 1.000 soldiers and civilians from the column were killed. After they committed this crime, the Chetniks called for surrender or negotiations. As the source emphasises on that occasion, Ejub Golic shouted back to the Chetniks requesting them to stop shelling, after which they stopped shelling the columns of soldiers and civilians." Can you follow? "Once the shelling stopped, the 284th Brigade gathered from the surrounding woods and continued on its way to the free territory, whereas, other brigades remained in the woods after the 284th Brigade had left." If another several persons said the one and the same thing and they were interviewed in various state security centres that 1.000 soldiers were killed where Ejub Golic negotiated with the Chetniks, if there were five persons who gave such statements in five different centres [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If various persons talk about one and the same event, and if the information is matching, then it is to be expected that this is the truth. But this is one location and one incident. It shouldn't turn out that only 1.000 perished in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Due to the length of this document, I did not want to read out the entire note to you. The Trial Chamber has already heard this. The statements of all these five witnesses have been presented to the Trial Chamber. You said that it is sufficient if three witnesses confirm one and the same event, which took place in the same place, and here we have five. As the place mentioned here, as you can see in line 8, is 8 kilometres, he says exactly after they passed another 8 kilometres, then there were roll-calls according to brigades. So he says exactly where the location was where Ejub Golic, about whom you have heard in the film a little while ago, when the other one said he needs to be awarded the rank of general because he managed to break through and so on. Can you tell us now whether you ever heard that anyone received requests from the Muslims through the ICRC or someone else, that these 1.000 bodies should be collected from this location and transported to the territory of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had intensive talks with the other side, that is to say, with the commission of the Tuzla canton, but about those who were imprisoned. As for those who were dead, they never mentioned those from this event until the moment when the commission was disbanded. They probably knew that we couldn't do anything about it, because this was the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, rather than the Eastern Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I've some problem with this kind of questions. It was a rather compact and confusing question. I couldn't follow, especially because we don't have an English translation. We saw the figure of 8 kilometres at a certain line, but that was all. You made a misstatement or you just misspoke, I have no idea, that in the 13th line from above, there -- that there would be the number of 10.000 and underlined in black. I only see the number of thousand, as you later quoted from this document. This is all in -- on page 18, lines 23 to page 19, line 5. This is really a way, putting an information to the witness, which bears the risk of confusing the witness, especially we don't know anything about this note, as you call it, we have on the screen. The document doesn't contain a date. We don't know the source. We don't know anything. And the witness was not testifying about this document but only about his general knowledge, how to receive information about the truth at certain locations. You put to the witness the name of Mr. Gajub [sic], I think, if I'm not mistake. I have no idea which person you are referring to. Perhaps you leave the document as it is and just put one question after the other to the witness. It is much more helpful to understand the position of the witness. Thank you, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is true that I misspoke when I said the number. These were 1.000 soldiers, and five such statements were presented to another witness, where 1.000 soldiers in this location are mentioned as having died. It's mentioned in the video footage that they were killed in an ambush, and I'm asking him whether the Muslim side ever asked that these bodies be brought out of there. I wanted to hear what happened with the bodies, because Mr. Thayer asked him whether he dealt with the exchange of the bodies of those who had been killed. It's on page 2, line 6. But then I won't ask anything else about this, either this witness or anyone else because it is already part of the evidence. And I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wish to thank Mr. Witness on the answers he provided. I apologise for having to ask you about some things that I asked you about and that you felt uncomfortable answering about some issues. I told you that I also feel uncomfortable to have to defend myself from accusations. But that's the situation, you're a witness; I'm the accused. So thank you. I wish you a happy return home. God bless you, and I hope you will enjoy your retirement. Thank you, and I wish you a happy return home.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Defence has no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to state for the record that I didn't stop you with your cross-examination. I wanted to give you some guidance to improve your cross-examinations so that we are able to understand better the position of the witness. That was the only purposes of my intervention. My last words were "please carry on." So there should be no misunderstanding. I didn't stop you at all. You stand by that, that you are finishing your cross-examination? Is that correct, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That's correct, I have finished my examination. And I wish the witness happy return home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, I just want to clarify one more thing with the witness. Did you receive any requests from the Bosnian side, or any other side, for that matter -- I need to rephrase this question. Yeah, did you receive any request for bodies to be picked along the line of the column that has been shown in the video footage? Or were such bodies reported to your commission? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On a number of occasions, we tried to get the bodies of those who were killed from the column, but we did not achieve this. While I was in the army, we never managed to get a single body of a single JNA soldier. Only much later, another commission received the mortal remains in an exchange, and they were buried in the area of the Tuzla cemetery, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Mitrovic, amongst the Muslim prisoners that you exchanged, did you count among them injured people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Now, when we talk about these injured people, were there any people who may have injured themselves while they were trying to escape? Would they have injured themselves either with a hand-grenade or with a weapon, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there were such individuals because I did not interview them. They were probably interviewed where the unit was located, from the area of the Drina Corps that they were brought from. I talked to them all about what the Tuzla Commission requested from their personal information, to the unit that they served in, down to the details, which brigade, which company, which platoon, and so on, because the Tuzla Commission wanted to be convinced and to be able to check whether they were really all soldiers of Naser Oric's unit. So that was only the segment that I was in charge of. I went one day to Batkovic. I placed a desk in the middle of the hall, and one by one, I asked them and I asked them to tell me the truth because the exchange commission from the Tuzla canton was asking me to do that, and I didn't ask them anything else apart from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time, I would like to ask the Defence, Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Gajic, how you want to deal with these footages we have seen during cross-examination. My suggestions would be that you upload them as a separate document in e-court, with a transcript and a translation into English and with a CD. If are you going to tender this part of the -- I think, trial video, we would mark it for identification. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the time being, I would ask for this to be marked for identification. And the transcript of this video footage is being produced. We will use it again with other witnesses, and we will also try to put subtitles on to the entire video footage. Unfortunately, Defence does not have such good technical abilities as the Prosecution, but we'll do our best to achieve this, as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The parts of the video we have seen in court today will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D801 shall be assigned Exhibit D280, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, again, pending translation, and providing the other information we asked for. Thank you. Mr. Thayer, your re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I shouldn't be too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to go back to a couple of issues which were raised on cross-examination, very specific issues, and to some extent, they overlap with the two questions from the Honourable Judges that you just heard. Let me first focus on the issue of any wounded or injured Muslim prisoners who arrived at the Batkovic camp in July of 1995. You testified - and this is at page 15.175, just for the record, yesterday -- you testified that the chief of security, Colonel Todorovic, informed you that a group of 20 wounded men from Srebrenica had arrived. Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you two documents in succession very quickly and ask you some questions about these wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have P2185 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast; it's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what we have before us is a document dated the 18th of July, 1995. It's a list of persons to be transferred under guard and it indicates the 3rd Battalion of the Eastern Bosnia Corps military police being involved and that this happened at about 4.00 p.m. on the 18th of July. We can see that there are 22 names here. And just for the purposes of looking at the next document, I just want to note and put this in your mind. If we look at number 4, we have the name of a person whose last name begins with A; I won't put it in the record. At number 9, another person with the last name A. Number 10, another person with the last name of -- beginning with A. 12, same thing. And 19, same thing. All persons whose last name begins with A. I just want to see if you can see that in this document, sir, before I move to the next document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have D228 in e-court. And I believe this is also under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown this document yesterday by General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is a list of Muslims exchanged from the Batkovic collection centre. And it's roughly organised alphabetically, and I think we noted yesterday that there were 171 prisoners listed on this chart. Sir, if you could just like at numbers 1 through 5. We can see that those first five individuals are the same individuals we just saw on the list of prisoners who were escorted by the Eastern Bosnia Corps military police, all names beginning -- last names beginning with A. Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly move away from the microphones. We pick up the B/C/S coming from the headphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we can scroll towards the right in both versions, please. There's a column and it's headed: "Date of arrival at Batkovic." Do you see that column, sir? And it lists various dates.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you see that for those first five individuals, their date of arrival is all 18 July 1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, how does that date of 18 July correspond with your recollection of when this group of 20 wounded who you testified about arrived at the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall when that group arrived. I do recall what I was told, though. But I didn't have time to go to either Batkovic or to the corps. I had to work under some extraordinary circumstances because of the requests and demands made by the parents of those missing. I don't know whether they all arrived on the same day, but I do remember that on a certain day they told me that there were 20 wounded from Srebrenica who had arrived and that I could go on with an exchange. I said that I couldn't because I needed at least the number of our captured soldiers to have them exchanged. I don't know if all 20 of them arrived at the same time. I didn't check.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't think there will be any dispute, and we don't need to take the time now to do it. But if you recall the list of wounded who we just saw a moment ago being escorted by the Eastern Bosnia Corps military police, every one of those names appears on the list you're looking at now and is recorded as having arrived on the 18th of July, 1995. And we could go and compare every one, but you can take my word for it, and I don't think there will be any dispute from the Defence that that is the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I would propose that we put the two documents in B/C/S side by side so that you have the names of these five individuals in both documents, and the witness can compare them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, my question, sir, is: We can go through both of these lists, and I can tell you that all 22 prisoners on this list on the right are recorded on the Batkovic list on the left as having arrived on the 18th of July, 1995. Does that help your recollection at all about what date you were told that those 20 wounded arrived, that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't told when they were coming. I was just told that 20 wounded had arrived and that there were no more. I was also told that I could have them exchanged with Tuzla. I can't recall the date, and I don't know whether they arrived on the same day I was informed about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just one last question with respect to the list on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can get rid of the list on the right, please. And we'll need to scroll to the right on the list on the left so we can pick up the column that's headed: "Date of departure from Batkovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you see the column that's headed "date of departure from Batkovic"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look down that column, we see a number of entries for 12 September 1995. We see one at the second entry, and then the fourth, and fifth entries, and so on, if you just look down that column. Do you see those references to 12 September 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday that your recollection is that some or perhaps all - I can't remember whether you specified - of the Lisace prisoners were exchanged on the 29th of September, 1995. My question to you is: This date here that indicates that these prisoners left on the 12th of September, 1995, does that suggest that they were exchanged on the 12th of September, 1995, or that they simply left the camp on the 12th of -- 12th of September, 1995, and were exchanged later; or can you not tell? That's my first question. I guess I'm just asking you to explain, if you would.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you recall, yesterday I mentioned that the 1st Krajina Corps asked for all prisoners from the area of Srebrenica to be transferred to the prison in Kotorsko, near Doboj, i.e., to the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps. I don't need to repeat what the problems arose -- that arose from it. In any case, we came up with a solution which was that we gave them between 40 and 50 prisoners, to have those exchanged in addition to a number of their captured Muslims, in order to have them exchanged for the people from Vijenac. In any case, that exchange did not occur. This was the date they left Batkovic but they were not exchanged with the other side, and they awaited the next one, a joint exchange, on the 24th of December. So those from Lisace were exchanged, and these people remained in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were asked a number of questions by General Tolimir about whether your commission had ever received any requests from the Muslim side to locate the bodies of Muslims who died during the break-through along the column route through Baljkovica. And the Honourable Judge Nyambe asked a somewhat similar question about whether you had received again a request regarding bodies killed -- or bodies of people killed along the column. I understand from your several answers on that topic that you never received - that is, your commission never received - any requests, because those -- such a request would have had to go through the Drina Corps POW Exchange Commission. Do I understand your answers correctly? And, if not, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received a request. We couldn't even expect one. They could have sent it to the Drina Corps Commission, given the good working relation between them, to see whether anything could be done. But they were probably aware that it would be very difficult to do anything. Hence, they didn't ask me or they didn't look for those killed in the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, the route of the column leading from the area of Srebrenica up through Baljkovica, does any of that route lie in the area of responsibility of the Eastern Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in connection with your work on the POW commission for -- for the Eastern Bosnia Corps, does the name, does the surname Novakovic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's someone who is a politician. Then there's another one in the army. There's some doctors and ambassadors who have that last name. You'll have to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll be more specific. Pardon me. Does the name Slavko Novakovic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move along, then, to my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. President, I think I -- I can stop here. I think I don't have any further questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And thank you again, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination here in this trial. The Chamber would like to thank you that you were able to come to The Hague again and to provide us with your knowledge and recollection. You're now free to return to your normal life and your normal activities. Thank you very much again. I think it is a convenient time to have our first break now, and then we will continue with the next witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before the next witness is being brought in, I would like to come back to an issue raised on the 25th of May this year. The Chamber made an order regarding the part of the session at which two videos were discussed. These are P2242 and P2228. The Chamber ordered that the status of this part of the session be changed from private to public. I should like to clarify that this order should be understood as applying to the audio and video recordings as well as the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is correct. Your understanding is correct. It should apply both to the transcript and to the exhibits themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And to the audio and video recordings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The next witness is ready to go, Mr. President. However, I do have an application that I'd like to make with respect to this witness. And I think it might be appropriate to go into private session, just initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please stand for a moment. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. On the request of the Prosecution, I have to caution you. We have in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence the Rule 90(E), which I would like to read out to you. I quote: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Sir, did you understand what I was just reading out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, for the Prosecution, is now putting questions to you during his examination-in-chief. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Your Honours, and good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Witness. I do have to ask you to state your name for the record. So if you would, please, just give us your name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Zoran Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall being interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 14th of December, 2005?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did that interview take place in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it took place at the ICTY office in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the interview tape-recorded?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I know that it was audio-recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And before testifying here today, have you had an opportunity to read the transcript of that interview?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: During the interview with the investigators at the ICTY office in Belgrade, I was told that I would receive the transcript and the audio-recording several days later. However, I only received the transcript last Tuesday, when someone from your office came to my door and handed this over to me. Also, yesterday, during conversation with you, you gave me the transcript, to read it, and state any objections I may have, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the -- your examination of the transcript, did you find any substantive errors, as opposed to what you might consider technical errors in the transcript. In other words, does it basically say what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Essentially it does. We removed some errors yesterday, but they were mostly technical by nature, and the interpreter told me that the transcript in English is correct and that there were some errors in translation into the Serbian language, and that this fact - that there was a translation - accounted for the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just before we get started, let me ask you: Do you stand by what you said during that December 2005 interview?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: On 14th of December, 2005, the interview was conducted practically ten and a half years after the events about which I gave my statement, or, rather, six or five and a half years before today's date. Many information appeared in the media in the meantime so that sometimes I wonder whether I said certain things in accordance with my recollection or under the impression of the stories about the period which were broadcast in the media. Therefore, 100 per cent certainty concerning certain events and certain conversations, primarily the conversations, whether I talked to certain persons or not, is something that I cannot provide. I cannot say with 100 percent certainty whether something happened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Can you say with 100 percent certainty that what appears in the transcript substantively is what you said during the course of the interview?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes. With 100 per cent certainty, what I said and stated in 2005, when I was interviewed at the ICTY office, is what appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just ask: Having read the transcript as recently as yesterday, is there anything in the transcript that you read substantively that you said to yourself, This is incorrect, or this is wrong, what I said then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Substantively, no. What the transcript contains is what I said in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. A little earlier you were asked some questions about your background and I just want to follow up with that a little bit. You indicated that you are engaged in some business now. Can you tell us, just for the record, because we have some of this, basically what you do these days, as a business?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: These days, or, rather, in the last two to three years, I do video production. That includes filming and video editing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated that you were a retired military officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I retired in 2002. I didn't do that, but I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: From what unit did you retire in 2002?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: May I ask you just one question, if it is not a problem? As I received approval from the state to talk about the period from December 1995, or, rather, until December 1995, and I'm not sure if I would have to bear any consequences if I talk about the later period. Namely, I was provided with this waiver to state something that is otherwise secret. I am not a legal professional, and, therefore, I'm asking you whether my answers concerning my career after 1995 and everything else that happened after that year, would entail any consequences on me from the state I live in and whose citizen I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, as you know I'm not a lawyer from Serbia, so I can't answer that question definitively. I can, however, request from the Trial Chamber to go into private session, which may resolve your concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to greet Mr. Malinic and wish him a pleasant stay here. If Mr. Vanderpuye is interested in what he did after the war, then he should go into closed session, if he really wants to know what the man did. And then in open session, he should put only those questions which include the period up to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that was the common understanding. Mr. Vanderpuye, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, can you give us a brief chronology of your military career. For example, did you start your military career by completing a mandatory service? What training and education that you got up until, let's say, we'll go through 1995, and then we can end there and pick up.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in Sarajevo. In 1986, I continued my education at the military high school Bratstvo and Jedinstvo in Belgrade. I completed that in 1980 when I joined the land forces academy in Belgrade. I completed the first two years following general courses, following which I specialised in infantry. I continued this part of my education in Sarajevo, where the third and fourth year of the Military Academy could be attended at the centre of military schools. I completed the Military Academy in 1984 as the first -- as the fourth in my class. Following that, I was sent to serve in Zagreb, in the 140th Infantry Regiment. I was appointed commander of the support platoon. I remained in the regiment for a month and a half, following which, I was moved to the sabotage detachment of the 5th Army. I remained there until 1987. Then I was transferred to the duty of commander of the motorised company in the 140th Infantry Brigade. It was in the Marshal Tito Barracks. It was basically transformed from the 140th Infantry Regiment to the 140th Motorised Brigade. I remained there until 1989 when I was appointed commander of the military police battalion in Varazdin. I remained in that position until June 1991. In that month, I was appointed assistant commander for morale in the same MP battalion. I stayed in Varazdin until September 1991 when the conflict began. On that occasion, together with a group of five officers and seven soldiers, I was captured in the Trinaesti Maj Barracks by the ZNG forces. My capture lasted for five to seven days when we were transferred to the territory of Slovenia without any documents, which were taken away during combat. I went to Sarajevo via Klagenfurt in Austria and then later on to Belgrade. I reported in Belgrade in October 1991. I was then assigned to the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment which at the time was in Slunj. It's a military training ground close to the town of Slunj in the territory of Croatia. From Slunj, we were transferred, or relocated, rather, first to Banja Luka and then to Kiseljak, where we arrived in late 1991. In March, the command and the protection regiment moved from Kiseljak to Butile near Sarajevo. During that period of 1992, I was without specific duty between October of the previous year and February of that year. I had no official appointment, since no order to that effect came my way. In March 1992, I was appointed deputy commander of the Sabotage Detachment of the 5th Army, where I remained until the 8th or 9th of May -- or, rather, until the end of May 1992. The Sabotage Detachment was a unit which suffered many casualties in Sarajevo. A part of the unit was stationed in the military hospital to provide security. When they tried to reach the command post on the 2nd of May, they were ambushed by the forces of the Muslim army, or, paramilitary units, because their army did not exist at the time. Seven soldiers and five officers were killed in that event, and there were a number of wounded. An officer remained in the hospital who was in charge of the communications department. He was the sole survive. Out of the group which managed -- which tried to reach the 1st Army command, only a platoon leader and three soldiers survived. On the 8th of May, 1992, we received an order for the remainder of the 65th [Realtime transcript read in error "56th"] Protection Regiment, that is to say, those who had not been captured or killed, to relocate to Han Pijesak, i.e., to the command post of the VRS. On the 8th of May, we arrived in Crna Rijeka, where we stayed until 1997. Between 1992, as of July of that year, I believe, actually, at that time, since there were very few soldiers and officers left, I was appointed MP battalion commander. I remained in that position until 1996 or early 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. First, I think we may have a translation or transcription error which is at page 51, line 14. There is a reference there to the 56th Motorised Protection Regiment. Can you tell us did you say that, or did you mean the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: 65th Motorised Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I thank you for clarifying that. I'm going to ask you a little bit about that unit. But, first, let me ask you: Do you now -- or did you know General Tolimir during the period of time that you served with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I met General Tolimir in May 1992 upon our arrival in Crna Rijeka. The 65th Protection Regiment was the first unit to arrive in Crna Rijeka. The officers who later comprised the Main Staff arrived later. I think we met in mid-May 1992. I had not known him before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And how would you characterise, if you can, briefly, your professional relationship with General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: My duty was that of the MP battalion commander. In certain intervals I also performed the duty of the regiment commander. Those intervals were very short. They are not that important. As I said, I met General Tolimir in May 1992. I treated him as my superior officer from a superior command, because the commander of the Main Staff was the immediate superior to the 65th Protection Regiment. I treated him with full respect, as an officer of a senior command. He treated me as an officer who was at the helm of the MP battalion, which was a unit intended to provide immediate security for the Main Staff and the rear command post of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, page 53, line 16, I think there is a word extra. It says "my superior officer." I don't think the witness said "superior," or at least I didn't hear it in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, it says "my superior officer." It is recorded like that. What is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness only said [In English] "officer from superior command." [Interpretation] And not "my superior officer, from my superior command." In military parlance, I think there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Malinic, can you help us? You treated General Tolimir as your superior. What is your -- what was your correct answer? Please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I treated General Tolimir as someone who was an officer from a superior command. He was a member of the Main Staff. I said that the immediate superior of the 65th Protection Regiment was the commander of the Main Staff, General Ratko Mladic. General Tolimir was a member of the superior command and not my superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What was General Tolimir's position during the time you served as the commander of the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir performed the duty of assistant commander for security and intelligence, at least to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned that he was a member of the Main Staff. What was the nature of the 65th -- the relationship of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment to the Main Staff of the VRS, in 1995, so that we can be a little bit more specific.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: As of 1992, when the VRS was established, the Main Staff had the same relationship to their regiment; that is to say, the relationship between the two instances was the same as in 1995. It was a unit of the Main Staff whose basic task was to physically secure the command post, as well as to secure the rear command post of the Main Staff, and to provide security to their personnel in movement or when still. By saying this, I have in mind those members of the Main Staff who were entitled to such protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: About how many people, how many soldiers made up the 65th Protection Regiment in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: In 1995, the protection regiment was comprised of the units of the command of the regiment, the logistics company, the protection battalion, which was formed, I believe, in 1994, which had a role to provide security in the general area of the command post, then the military police battalion, which was the only unit that was in operation as of 1992. Next, there was the sabotage detachment of the 65th Protection Regiment. As for the number of people and staffing levels on our lists, that is something I can't say with any certainty. I can only speak of the battalion of the military police, not of the entire regiment. Whatever I said might be wrong in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'm not looking for a figure to quote you on, but I just want the Trial Chamber to have a sense of how big or small the regiment was. So can you approximate how many people were in the regiment or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Let's say approximately 700 people, including all the units. But that is based on the lists and the number of people on those lists. This also included those soldiers who had been wounded or were on sick-leave or who were being treated, as well as those soldiers who were incapable of taking up their duties but were still members of the regiment so that they could exercise certain rights as members of the VRS. We couldn't simply delete them from the list of the regiment. Although, in real terms, they were unable to participate in any combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And the units that you listed for us before, are these all of the units that comprised the 65th Protection Regiment in 1995? That is, you have listed the command, logistics, the protection battalion, the military police battalion, and the sabotage detachment. Are these all the units that comprised the regiment in July of 1995, to be specific?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I think I forgot to say that there was an anti-aircraft battalion as part of the 65th Protection Regiment. I think this includes all the units that were part of the regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Under whose command was the regiment - direct command - was the regiment in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there seems to be another problem with military terminology, namely, page 56, lines 17 and 18. There's a mention of "battalion" -- sorry. No, line 21, line 22, "anti-aircraft battalion." I think the witness said "division."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Artillery battalion is what in the Serbian language is "protu avionski divizion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you may follow up with it or it should be checked later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it can probably be checked later. It's not that critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I think I just asked you whose direct command the regiment was under in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: The regiment was under the command of -- well, not in 1995, but as of 1992, it was under direct command of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Mladic. The immediate superior to the 65th Protection Regiment was General Mladic, Commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the regiment in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment was, I think, Lieutenant-Colonel, or Colonel, Milomir Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned in one of your answers the command of the regiment. Can you tell us who the members of the command of the regiment were in July 1995, aside from Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff of the regiment was Lieutenant-Colonel Jovo Jazic. The chief of the training and education department was Lieutenant-Colonel Vojislav Sarovic. The assistant commander for logistics was Captain Slijepcevic, first name Predrag. The chief of the security organ, I think, was Captain Ruskic, although I'm not certain. I think he was the chief of the security organ of the regiment at the time. I think that's it, as the regiment command goes in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now you were the commander of the military police battalion in July 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what relationship, if any, did you have with the superior organ for security in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff security organ was a specialised organ which managed the work of the military police unit in the professional sense. They were in charge of the professional and expert side. They provided guide-lines to the military police battalion. As far as I can remember, the Main Staff security organ did not have a chief in charge of military police at the time. In July 1995, Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic was appointed to that position, and until that time, he had discharged the duty of commander of the military police battalion in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did your unit - the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment - have contact with the security organ of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: My unit did have contacts with the security organ of the Main Staff from the time when the Main Staff was set up. That is to say, from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what was the nature of the contact that your unit had with the Main Staff security organ in 1995? For example, whom did you have contact with, about what matters you had contact, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: The military police battalion, according to the rules of service pertaining to military police, had to secure the rear command post to provide protection to persons whether they are stationary or moving, but in wartime, a military police battalion, in other words, that was in a period between 1992 and the end of the war, the proper use of military police was not observed, primarily because the use of the military police battalion, or, actually, the military police battalion was used for -- to carry out combat operations and discharge other duties and tasks which were not prescribed by the instructions on the work of military police and the rules of service for military police. The nature of the contacts with the security organs of the Main Staff was such that the security organs influenced the command, which made decisions, primarily the Main Staff command, on the use of the military police battalion. If I may add, the military police battalion was used many times as a unit which had to carry out offensive or defensive combat operations, which was not the proper use of this unit. And as the commander of the military police battalion, I requested from the Main Staff security organs, considering this, that such tasks, which were not part of the normal use of military police, should be reduced to a minimum, and that was mainly the nature of our contacts. On the other hand, security organs were charged as professional organs of the military police. They were in charge of equipping military police with equipment needed for carrying out military police tasks. They were the only ones who were in charge of supplies. This was part of the description of duties of those security organs. I would also add that we contacted security organs on receiving tasks that were military police tasks by character, primarily suppressing certain groups which were out of control. These were units in the field. And by order of the Main Staff, or the commander of the regiment, we were sent to carry out such tasks.
