That was when we had the closest cooperation with security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Part of my question was: Whom did you deal with? Did you deal with the assistant commander for security and intelligence, General Tolimir, at the Main Staff level? Did you deal with Colonel Beara at the Main Staff level? Did you deal with General Keserovic - now-General Keserovic - at that level? Or all three?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: As for General Tolimir, we had most contacts with him in the first period; that is to say, from the arrival of the Main Staff to the command post, from 1992, May 1992, up until November 1992, I think. As far as I remember, I think that he was the only security organ at the time who was at the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Colonel Beara, to my recollection, only arrived later, in late 1992. It was only then in late 1992 that I personally met Colonel Beara. Further contacts connected with the work of military police were mainly with Colonel Beara. It was only at the time of Mr. Beara, or, rather, Colonel Beara's absence, because I think very few people worked in the security department of the Main Staff, and from this point in time, I cannot remember who else, in addition to Colonel Beara, was working for the Main Staff security department. Colonel Keserovic, who is today a general, I had my first contact with him in July 1995. I had the pleasure of meeting him then, and I had heard about him earlier because he was the commander of the military police battalion in the 1st Corps; that is to say, in Banja Luka. I think that before that, he was also a commander -- he was the commander of the military police battalion in Bijeljina, but we had no chance to meet personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As the commander of the military police battalion in July 1995, from whom did you receive your orders?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: The military police battalion received orders from the command of the 65th Protection Regiment Command. I think it was Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic, or he was perhaps a colonel at the time. I cannot remember. So it was the command of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment that issued our orders to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you receive orders from the command of the Main Staff directly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: In 1995, the battalion was in several locations. One group from the MP battalion was securing the command post and the rear command post, which was reinforced in late June 1995, when the Muslim forces from Zepa attacked the command post. So one part of the unit was there. Another part of the unit was in the Sarajevo sector, where it was resubordinated to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That part of the unit was commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel Sarovic. He was one of the officers from the regiment who was there. First name Vojislav. This part of the unit received their tasks from the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I think that they had a forward command post in the Trnovo sector. A third part of the military police battalion was in Kasaba, where, after the fighting on Treskavica in June 1995, and where we had sustained great losses, it was an offensive launched by the Muslim forces on Sarajevo, and I was there with a part of the unit. In the period between the 17th and the 20th of June, that part of the unit, which was led by me, sustained losses. More than one-third of the unit was no longer fit for fighting. I think that we had more than 100 wounded and number of dead soldiers. It was the Muslim offensive, which had begun on 15th of June, and the location where we were in the Treskavica mountain sector, there it began on the 17th of June. In Kasaba, at the time, there were around 20 soldiers and officers, if we can call this the third part of the military police battalion, which was in the territory of Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it is the time for the second break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify one thing, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Malinic, was whether you received orders from the command of the Main Staff. And you have mentioned a unit that was under the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, I believe, a unit that was in Treskavica, and another unit that was in Kasaba. But, really, I'd just like to know did you receive orders from the command of the Main Staff? And that's -- if you received them directly. I'd just like to know if you can answer that with a yes or a no, since we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I gave you the explanation because you asked me whether I was receiving orders from the Main Staff. I wanted to describe to you the situation that the military police battalion was in during the months of June and July. The battalion was split into several groups, and as the commander of the battalion, I was unable to command the whole battalion. Orders for carrying out operations were something that I received from the command of the Protection Regiment primarily from Lieutenant-Colonel, or Colonel, Savcic, or in case of his absence, from the Chief of Staff, Jovo Jazic. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I could have expected that there is no yes or no to this question. We must have our second break now, and we will resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is everything okay there, Mr. Malinic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's okay. I was just thinking about your question during the break. I would note several exceptions which existed when it came to issuing certain orders. I primarily mean that, on several occasions, I went to receive the tasks directly from the Main Staff commander with Lieutenant-Colonel, or Colonel, Savcic. So I was present on these occasions when we were directly given our tasks. Primarily this happened in cases when I was the main commander responsible for carrying out certain tasks. In these cases, I received orders directly from the commander of the Main Staff. I just wanted to make this correction to what I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Let me just direct your attention to the 13th of July, 1995. Can you tell us where you were in the early morning of that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, 1995, I was in the barracks in Nova Kasaba. That is a school which was used as a school before the war. During the war, or, more precisely, in late 1993, it was turned into a facility or barracks for the accommodation of the members of the military police battalion of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have in e-court, please, P1157.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph, or this location, rather?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Can you just -- I see a road and several vehicles. Can you somehow make the background lighter? Because I can just see some white shapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, we've had this problem typically with the monitor that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Usher can assist the witness. It's the question of the angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah, if he stands up, he might be able to see it better, but there are ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the morning of the 13th -- of 13 July 1995, about how many soldiers were garrisoned at that school or billeted there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, 1995, around 20 soldiers with their officers, so counting them as well, were stationed at the school, or barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I take it these were -- these soldiers were members of your battalion, of your unit.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you at some point that day receive or capture Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when did you first come into contact with these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I came into contact with these prisoners for the first time during the morning. We were informed by - I'm not sure whether it was a woman or a man -- who came to the gate of the barracks, it's at the entrance at the side of the road, and said that he or she was coming from Konjevic Polje, and that many soldiers were crossing the road between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba. I then sent group [as interpreted] to see what this was about, and after a short while, they returned with several soldiers they had imprisoned. And these soldiers were Muslims by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You say "several soldiers." Can you approximate how many soldiers or individuals they returned with, after you'd sent them on the assignment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I think there were three prisoners. And that they reported to me that many members of the Muslim army were crossing the road from the direction of the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What did you do with these several soldiers that were brought back by your men?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: We accommodated them in a building next to the barracks, which was not a detention unit or a prison. It was a building which we used to repair motor vehicles, because there was a canal on the floor [as interpreted] of the building. It was made by the owner and it was probably prepared to become a car mechanics shop. It was a building which was outside the parameter of the barracks because the school itself was surrounded by a fence. This was a privately owned house, which was not a part of the school complex before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, I just need a clarification. At page 66, line 10, Mr. Vanderpuye asked you: "You say 'several soldiers.' Can you approximate how many soldiers or individuals they returned with after you had sent them on the assignment?" And your answer was: "I think there were three prisoners." In the next question, again, Mr. Vanderpuye says: "What did you do with these several soldiers." Can you clarify? Were there three soldiers, prisoners, or several? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there were three, but whether this is a correct number, it's hard to tell because so much time has passed. I think there were three. The group sent to see what the situation was, was a group of three soldiers. This is why I estimate that the number of prisoners was not bigger than three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I add another question to the same matter. You mentioned the three prisoners first, then you added: "And that they reported to me that many members of the Muslim army were crossing the road from the direction the woods." What is that about -- I really don't understand that sentence about "... many members of the Muslim army." How did you get to know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first information that units of the Muslim army were crossing the road was given to us by the person who was passing along that morning, along the road between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba and who stopped to inform us about this. The next information that this was a large number of soldiers was something I heard from the commander of the group which took these soldiers prisoners. So the information that there were many of Muslim army members is something I received from two sources. The first one was the person who reported this to us that morning, and the next time it was reported to me was by the commander of the group who had taken these three soldiers prisoner and brought them to the barracks. When I mentioned from the direction of the woods, that there was this column moving from there, it would be much easier if I could show you on a map where the area is. And when I say "from the woods," it is because when they crossed the road, it was an open space then, leading to the hills. This is why I mentioned "the woods."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you received these several prisoners, did you notify anyone concerning that, concerning what was going on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Of course. The first contact I made about this was with the command of the 65th Protection Regiment, located in Crna Rijeka. After that, I also informed the police in Milici. I wanted to inform them about a situation which existed in the territory of their municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you learn anything from the Milici police or from the command of the regiment concerning what was going on? In other words, did they tell you that they knew about the situation, that they didn't know about the situation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: From this point in time, I cannot exactly say what they said. But my reaction was to inform them, the command of the regiment primarily, about the numbers, the number of men who were in the barracks in Nova Kasaba. I also requested from the command of the regiment to send a part of my unit which was performing the role of reinforcing security for the command. I wanted them to be sent over and help me. And I contacted the police so that they would be aware of the situation in their territory and so that they could also provide me with some assistance, if they could. I think that they did not have any information about the situation on the ground and this came as surprise to both the command and the soldiers in this territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of the command - if you can recall - in Crna Rijeka, who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I think at the time in the regiment command, it was Lieutenant-Colonel, or Colonel, Jovo Jazic. He was the Chief of Staff of the regiment. Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic was absent from the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know where Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic was at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: My information was that he went to execute a task with a part of the unit in the direction of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you speak to Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: There is a great possibility that I did. If, indeed, we spoke, he probably called me because I simply didn't know at what number he could be reached and whether there were any possibilities to get in touch. When I say that there is a great possibility, I mean to say that it is most likely that we did speak. If I were to put it in terms of percentages, I'd say there is an 80 per cent chance we did speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'll accept that. Given that probability that you spoke, what would you have spoken about, or what did you speak about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: If we spoke, we probably discussed the situation in the field in the area of Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Where -- do you know where he was specifically at the time that you would have spoken to him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he was exactly. I wasn't familiar with his task or his axis or what location was included as part of that task of his in the direction of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: After you spoke to Colonel Jazic, or, rather, let me rephrase this. Did you speak to Colonel Jazic or to Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic on more than one occasion on the morning of 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I can't say with 100 per cent certainty that I did. But it would have been normal for me to speak to both Jazic and Savcic on a few occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said that you'd asked for reinforcements. Did you -- did you receive reinforcements that morning or at some point during the day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive reinforcements. Lieutenant-Colonel Jazic sent an APC company, or, rather, part of that company, headed by their commander, Zoran Benak, Lieutenant. In addition to that, the Main Staff sent a platoon from the communications regiment, which was located in Crna Rijeka as well, and which was under direct command from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you refer to the communications regiment, are you referring to the 67th Communications Regiment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had in mind the 67th Communications Regiment. I think it was the only communications regiment in the VRS, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this platoon from the communications regiment, did this consist of soldiers that were engaged in, or trained in, communications matters, or was this a combat unit from that regiment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I think the 67th Communications Regiment did not have a combat unit in its ranks. These people were soldiers who were primarily trained in communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you received this platoon, what did you assign them to do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: The communications platoon which came as a reinforcement was subordinated to me, in terms of command. Together with their officers, they were deployed along the blockade line in the field, along the route taken by the Muslim forces when executing their break-through.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you deploy this unit together with the unit -- the APC unit that Benak came with?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: The APC unit was not deployed along the blockade line. It was only the soldiers from that company who came there with their commander that were deployed. The APCs themselves, of which there were two, I think, were part of a group that we established once they arrived. The group was tasked to be in the area covered by the MP battalion, that is to say, the area that was sealed off, to intervene in case there was a successful attempt at break through in the area where we were. In other words, the APCs, the vehicles themselves, were not part of the blockade line. We had a contingency plan, that is to say, there was an intervention group which was to be used to intervene, if needed, along the route of break through by the Muslim forces. Of course, with those two APCs, there were also a number of personnel from that APC company.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How many soldiers came with that unit? Just to make it specific: How many came with that unit, together with Benak?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I don't think I can be specific as to any number, but anywhere between 40 and 50 soldiers who had arrived with Lieutenant Benak.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Around what time did these units arrive, the 67th Communications Regiment platoon and the unit that arrived with Benak?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I think it was before 9.00. That's when they arrived. Or maybe even earlier. Only once Benak was already there the part of the communications regiment that was sent arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Around what time did that unit arrive? That's the communications regiment platoon.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: The communications regiment platoon, I think an hour or two following Benak.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you continue to receive or capture prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I can see Jovo Jazic -- no, it's gone now. Since Benak arrived with his unit, we began expanding the blockade line towards the part of the route where the Muslim forces attempted break-through. Actually, it was not an attempt because up to that point, they moved unhindered without any resistance. It was our basic task to close the gap and to prevent any further advancement of the Muslim forces towards the area they intended to use for their passage. It took place gradually. And as we were expanding the line, we managed to capture a certain number of Muslims as part of that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P663.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should be P663B.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's under seal, Mr. President, and so shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm showing you, sir, is a radio intercept that was captured by the 2nd Corps. And it's dated 13 July 1995. The time indicated here is 10.15 a.m., and it indicates participants Beara, Lucic, and Zoka. I know you have seen this before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this intercept earlier. Yesterday, the last time; and the first time was when I was in the Belgrade office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see at the very beginning of this intercept it says. "Beara speaking." And: "Hello, Signor Lucic, how are you?" Can you tell us, did you have an individual by the name of Lucic who was a member of your command, that is, the command of the military police battalion of the regiment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Lucic, or Captain Lucic, was my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was Captain Lucic - your deputy - present at Nova Kasaba on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: As per establishment of the MP battalion, Lucic had been assigned to the position of deputy commander. Before that, he had been the commander of a military police company. On the 13th of July, he was on leave, I believe. Since he lived nearby with his family, once we realised what the situation we were in was, all the officers and soldiers were urgently summoned to the barracks. I think Captain Lucic returned from his leave that very morning. We called him to come back. That is how he came to be in the area of the Nova Kasaba Barracks on the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we look a little bit further down here, we can see here - pardon me - that Beara says: "Do you hear me? Do you know that 400 balijas have shown up in Konjevic Polje?" And what's marked as attributed to Lucic says: "I know." Now, Konjevic Polje was approximately how far from the area where your battalion was garrisoned, or the school that you showed us just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I think it was 5 -- 4 or 5 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go through this conversation, you can see that Lucic and Beara exchange some information regarding the circumstances of the prisoners. And Beara says: "They have been rounded up, disarmed, everything?" And then we don't see an answer from Lucic. And Beara says: "Excellent, excellent, great. And there is someone to guard them?" And Lucic says: "There is ..." If we go to the -- I think we're on the same page. We'll have to go to the next page in English. And we can see that the conversation then turns to the group that Lucic is talking about, and he says just before this: "Over here, there's this huge group." Sorry, we'll have to go back a page in the English, to the bottom of the page. He says: "Here we have over here there's this huge group." And Beara says at the very bottom of the page, he says: "Well, you can also, those 20, so that the forces are not dispersed. Shove them all on the playground, who gives a fuck about them?" And then if we go to the next page, Beara says: "They're locked up, right?" And then follows with: "Do you have enough room over there?" What I first want to ask you is: Where Beara refers to these 400 balijas, is he referring to the Muslims, prisoners, in Konjevic Polje? Is that how you understand it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: I understand it this way. Colonel Beara asked Lucic if he knew that 400 balijas came out in Konjevic Polje. Lucic responded by saying, I do. I am not sure whether Captain Lucic could have information about what was going on in Konjevic Polje because the road between Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje was cut off. And I don't think we had any means of communication, either by radio or telephone with Konjevic Polje to receive any kind of information. An engineering battalion was stationed in Konjevic Polje from the Drina Corps. In this conversation, I don't see a possibility of Captain Lucic providing this information or confirming that he was aware of the 400 Muslims who came out in Konjevic Polje. I don't know how he could have gotten hold of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Further on in this conversation, you will see that Beara starts to speak to someone by the name of Zoka. Is that you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: It probably is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Before that, he refers to putting these people on the playground. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what the playground is that Beara is referring to in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC
utterances.text: It's a soccer pitch next to the road as one enters Nova Kasaba from the direction of Konjevic Polje. It's a soccer pitch without any stands. There's just a grass field and a couple of small buildings that were probably used as changing rooms and a building for the referees during a match. It is some 300 metres away from the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know we are just about out of time. I can pick this up tomorrow, if you like, or I can finish this one exhibit, however you want to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you should continue tomorrow morning with this exhibit and with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom number III. You should be reminded that no contact with either party about the content of your testimony is allowed. Thank you very much. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
